# Share Your Code

## Reading 1

::: {.nonincremental}
- Title: **Top ten reasons to not share your code (and why you should anyway)**
- Authors: Randall J. LeVeque.
- Journal: Software Sustainability Institute
- Year: 2012
- <https://www.software.ac.uk/blog/top-ten-reasons-not-share-your-code-and-why-you-should-anyway>
:::


## Reading 2

::: {.nonincremental}
- Title: **Publish your computer code: it is good enough**
- Authors: Nick Barnes.
- Journal: Nature 467 (7317): 753 
- Year: Oct 2010
- doi: 10.1038/467753a
- <https://doi.org/10.1038/467753a>
:::


# Discussion Time

## Screens Off, Minds On

\

::: {.nonincremental}
- [Devices Away:]{.bold-hilit} Laptops & tablets closed, phones away.

- [No One Alone:]{.bold-hilit} Pair or team up (no solo seats).

- [Engage Fully:]{.bold-hilit} Be ready to speak, debate, and share ideas.
:::


## Poll

\

::: {.poll}
Have you ever read a paper, wanted the code and/or the data, 
emailed the authors asking for it "upon request," and received nothing back?
:::

. . .

\

Write your answer on the scrath paper handed out to you.


## The "Demand Support" Excuse

Common excuse to not share code: <br>
["People will pick holes and demand support."]{.bold-hilit}

\

- Suppose you've written an R/Python package that you want to share via GitHub.
- You are worried that users will demand technical support.

. . .

::: {.poll}
Silently think (and write) about two boundaries that you would set to limit how much support 
you are willing to give.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(3, bottom = 0)
```


## Drafting a `SUPPORT.md` file

Common excuse to not share code: <br>
["People will pick holes and demand support."]{.bold-hilit}

\

. . .

::: {.poll .nonincremental}
- In trios, draft a `SUPPORT.md` disclaimer for a GitHub repo. 

- State your commitment to open science while setting firm boundaries 
against personal tech support requests.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(5, bottom = 0)
```


## Discussion (part 1)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Team A: The Proprietary Tech Firm]{.hilit}

- Your team has built a simulation code that calculates the structural stress limits 
for public bridges. 
- Your team refuses to share the code claiming it's a corporate secret.
:::

::: {.column width="5%"}
:::

::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}
[Issues]{.bold-hilit}

- A bridge design built using the firm's secret code has just shown minor structural cracks. 
- The firm claims it's an isolated steel issue, not a software issue.
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.poll}
Huddle with your immediate neighbors to formulate 3 compelling arguments to defend 
Team A position.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(4.5, bottom = 0)
```

## Discussion (part 3)

The tech firm ([Team A]{.hilit}) refuses to open-source its proprietary stress-testing code 
due to commercial secrets.

But the public safety board ([Team B]{.mdlit}) refuses to trust a black box.

\

. . .

::: {.poll}
How can Team A prove its code works without leaking its competitive edge to global rivals?
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(4.5, bottom = 0)
```
